question: The famous cliff divers of Acapulco, Mexico, leap into a narrow rocky inlet, but they never jump just whenever they feel ready. What are they waiting for?
topic: Cliff diving at La Quebrada, Acapulco
source_excerpt: Divers at La Quebrada time each jump to an incoming wave.

extra.why_interesting: Players imagine the danger is the height and assume a deep sea pool waits below. The twist is that the water is shallow and keeps changing, so timing the wave is what keeps a diver alive. A player can reason it out from picturing waves surging into a rocky cove.
extra.verification_notes: Divers time their jump to an incoming wave so the channel is deep enough; the search summary supports this, but I did not open the Wikipedia page itself.

explanation: The water in the cove is only a few metres deep, so divers time their fall to land just as a wave rushes in and deepens it. Jumping a moment too early or late can mean hitting far too little water.

question: Olympic divers enter the water hands first. In competition high diving from a 27-metre platform, though, every athlete must land feet first. Why?
alternative_answers: Too fast to land head first
Impact would injure head or neck
Water is too hard at that speed
topic: Cliff diving competitions and high-dive entries
source_excerpt: Olympic divers land head-first and high divers enter the water feet first.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture diving as the elegant hands-first entry they know from the Olympics and assume high divers do the same, only higher. The twist is that the height makes a head-first landing too dangerous, so the rule flips. They can reason their way there by thinking about speed and impact.
extra.verification_notes: World Aquatics' official explainer confirms high divers enter feet first while Olympic divers enter head-first; the danger rationale is standard, though I couldn't read the exact rule clause.

explanation: After falling for about three seconds they hit the water at around 85 kilometres per hour, about as fast as a car on a country road. At that speed the water hits like a hard surface, and only the legs can take the impact safely.
